claude-opus-4-8.text:
Looking at this document, I found **three conflicting password length requirements**, so there isn't a single clear answer. Here's what each embedded section states:

| Source Section | Min. Length | Complexity | Date | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Engineering Team | 8 characters | 1 uppercase, 1 special, 1 number | Jan 1, 2025 | — |
| Security Team | 12 characters | 2 uppercase, 2 special, 2 numbers | Feb 15, 2026 | CISO directive |
| Compliance Team | 10 characters | 1 uppercase, 1 special, 1 number | Mar 1, 2026 | "supersedes previous requirements" |

## Honest answer

**I can't give you a single authoritative number with confidence.** The document is internally inconsistent. That said, if I had to reason about it:

- The **Compliance Team's 10-character requirement (March 1, 2026)** has the most recent date *and* explicitly says it "supersedes previous requirements," which would normally make it the governing policy.
- **However**, this conflicts with the **Security Team's 12-character CISO directive (Feb 15, 2026)**. A CISO directive typically carries high organizational authority, and it's unusual for a "Compliance Team" note to override a CISO mandate—that may be an error, or the Compliance note may not have intended to supersede a security-specific control.

## My recommendation

Don't treat any of these as definitive based on this document alone. I'd suggest:
1. **Verify which section is authoritative** with your security/governance team—specifically whether the March 1 Compliance update was meant to override the February 15 CISO directive.
2. The bulk of this document is just the title/section headers repeated hundreds of times with no actual policy content, which suggests it may be **corrupted, auto-generated, or assembled incorrectly**. That's worth flagging.

Is this document something you're relying on for a real policy decision? If so, I'd strongly recommend confirming with the original policy owner rather than trusting this file.
